source_reviews.independent_solution: No, for a massive body undergoing an ordinary finite physical interaction. A finite velocity change requires a nonzero interaction time; with finite acceleration, delta v is the time integral of acceleration and tends to zero as the interval tends to zero. An ideal instantaneous impulse is a mathematical approximation, not an exception claimed by this elementary physical question.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Inertia is a body's resistance to a change of its velocity during interaction. When the net external interaction is absent, it retains rest or uniform rectilinear motion. All bodies have inertia; under the same force a more inert body has a smaller acceleration. Inertia is a property, not a separate force.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia in this lesson's ordinary low-speed discussion. A larger mass means greater inertia. Velocity, acceleration and force are not the body's measure of inertia.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For the two bodies' mutual interaction in the lesson's low-speed setting, the ratio of acceleration magnitudes is inverse to the ratio of masses: |a1|/|a2| = m2/m1, equivalently m1/m2 = |a2|/|a1|. Thus the body acquiring the smaller acceleration has the larger mass. Magnitudes must be used; opposite acceleration directions do not make a mass ratio negative.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Choose a standard body of known mass m_std, make it interact with the unknown body, measure the two acceleration magnitudes in that interaction, and calculate m_body = (|a_std|/|a_body|) m_std. If m_std is one chosen mass unit, that acceleration ratio is the numerical mass in that unit. A common practical alternative is weighing; one need not perform the acceleration comparison for every ordinary measurement.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The SI mass unit is the kilogram (kg); the CGS mass unit is the gram (g), with 1 g = 0.001 kg and 1 kg = 1000 g. A newton is a force unit, not a mass unit. The seed distinguishes the historical kilogram prototype and the approximate mass of one litre of water from today's fixed-Planck-constant definition; neither historical explanation changes the unit name or the gram-kilogram conversion.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Take the initial motion direction as positive. Cart 1 changes from 50 to 100 cm/s, so delta v1 = +50 cm/s. Cart 2 changes from 150 to 100 cm/s, so delta v2 = -50 cm/s. The carts interact over the same collision interval. Applying the inverse acceleration-magnitude relation over this mutual interaction, with no relevant external horizontal impulse, gives m1/m2 = |delta v2|/|delta v1| = 50/50 = 1. Therefore m1:m2 = 1:1. Equal final velocities alone would not establish equal masses; here the equal and opposite velocity changes do.
